sentences.text: Vera found the eel in the third week, in one of the pools that were left in the mud, and she found it because she was doing the thing everybody at the caravan site was doing, which was walking about out there when the light went and it got cool enough.
The pool was maybe four metres across and knee-deep and warm as soup, and there were sticklebacks in it, and there was, along the bottom, an eel about as long as her arm.
She thought it was stuck.

That was her first thought and it was a reasonable one — there were fish stranded all over that mud in August, dying in shrinking puddles, and she had already carried two carp to the main channel and been extremely pleased with herself.
The carp had been horrible to carry.

They were enormous and they had gone quiet in the way a fish goes quiet, and one of them had come back to life halfway and nearly gone out of her arms, and she had walked the last thirty metres holding it against her chest like a baby with the mud sucking at her feet.
She had told nobody about the carp either.
It was that sort of August.
She got down on her knees and put her hands in.
The water was the temperature of a bath that has been left.

There was mud in it that came up in clouds the moment she moved, so that she had to wait between attempts for it to clear, kneeling in the warm with her sleeves pushed up and the sun going down behind the dam.
The eel did not want to be carried.
It went round her wrists twice and got out the other side and came back to almost exactly the place it had started, and settled, and looked at her, which eels can do more than people expect.
She tried again and the same thing happened.
The third time she stopped and sat back on her heels in the mud and looked at where the pool was.
She was not thinking anything clever.
She was thinking that she had been beaten by a fish and that her knees hurt.
It was in a straight line.
She had not noticed it because she had come at it from the side.

But standing up, in the low sun, with the shadows long, she could see that the pool she was kneeling in was one of about nine, in a row, running away from her towards the tower — and that the row was not a row of pools at all.
It was a street.
The pools were the low bits.
Between them, under a skin of dried mud, was the crown of a road, cambered, running from somewhere behind her all the way to the church.

She walked the length of it in the last of the light, out and back, four hundred paces one way, and where the crust was thin she could put her heel through it and there was stone underneath, laid stone, set on edge the way they used to set it.
